title: Safety and Resilience Strategies for Remote Medical Teleoperation: When Is AI-Enabled Local Autonomy Justified? A Narrative Review and Minimum Safe Autonomy Framework
content: Background/Objectives: Remote medical teleoperation can extend access to specialist care, yet failures of effective remote control pose patient-safety risks. This critical narrative review examines how protective responses should be selected for such failures and when local autonomy is justified. Methods: We synthesized selected clinical, preclinical, engineering, and consensus evidence on telesurgical safety, focusing on disturbance mechanisms, measured endpoints, human recovery, and protective control. Results: Clinical studies primarily demonstrate feasibility under prepared conditions, whereas direct evidence of protection during major disturbances is scarce. We introduce Minimum Safe Autonomy (MSA), a hazard-specific protective-autonomy assessment framework combining six functional categories (S0–S5) with a seven-stage evaluation. Rather than rank entire robots by autonomy, MSA documents a response-selection decision: the required patient–device safe state, available time before harm, feasible deterministic safeguards and human intervention, candidate local sensing or action, and the evidence supporting each option. The assessment yields three outcomes—an adequately supported response for specified conditions, a research candidate requiring further evidence, or redesign/non-deployment. Three hypothetical scenarios illustrate how S1 protection may suffice, S3 stabilization may merit investigation, and S2 blood perception alone does not authorize S4 treatment. Conclusions: MSA makes the rationale for selecting the least complex adequately justified protective response explicit within established risk-management approaches. Its incremental decision-making value and the safety of individual responses should be evaluated separately against established methods and patient-relevant physical outcomes.
